transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date: 2026-04-09
- Time: 15:30 PDT
- Duration: 47 minutes
- Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Raj Patel (Redwood SE), Emily Stone (Head of ML - Orchard AI), Diego Ramos (VP Eng), Priya Narayanan (Infra Lead)

Summary (auto): quick intake to verify isolation and burst requirements, follow ups to share heatmaps and pilot pricing.

[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone thanks for joining, we got about 45 minutes so we'll do quick intros, then dive into traffic and isolation needs. Uh, Raj and I will jump over the technical bits.
[00:12] Emily Stone: Thanks Maya. Quick note, we're evaluating three options: hosted for dev, dedicated for prod, and possibly private on-prem later. Primary concern is isolation for PHI-adjacent embeddings and consistent p99 latency under load.
[00:30] Raj Patel: Got it. When you say PHI-adjacent, are embeddings actually storing identifiers or just derived features?
[00:36] Emily Stone: It's mostly derived but sometimes we have patient IDs hashed in metadata. Compliance wants strong tenant fencing and customer-managed keys where possible.
[01:05] Diego Ramos: And from infra side, we need predictable throughput around our heavy hours — roughly 80 to 120 qps for small chat completions and bursts up to ~350 qps for short windows. Cost is a big driver so we prefer reservation + spot-like burst.
[01:30] Maya Chen: That's the pattern we see a lot. Reserved nodes for baseline, then burst into hot pool or prewarmed spot capacity. We have a few levers: dedicated GPU pools, warm-pool pre-warms, and automated fallback to smaller quantized variants.
[01:50] Priya Narayanan: Can you explain the fallback flow? If a reserved node is saturated, how do you keep latency from spiking?
[02:04] Raj Patel: Sure — we do smart routing: first try reserved pool, if capacity constrained, we route to a compatible model variant in a different pool or in a lower-cost quantized flavor. There's also a prewarm hotpool that keeps a small number of nodes ready for rapid scale up.
[02:25] Emily Stone: Any chance we can dedicate physical isolation — like a tenant-only node group? We need to show auditors.
[02:35] Maya Chen: Yes, Dedicated supports tenant-level isolation: either fully isolated reserved clusters or a logical fencing model where only your jobs run on the nodes. For highest assurance, physical isolation in Dedicated is available.
[02:52] Diego Ramos: And network isolation? VPC peering or private control plane?
[02:58] Raj Patel: We offer a private control plane option for Dedicated deployments — control plane endpoints inside your VPC plus optional on-prem packaging. KMS/HSM integration is supported; you can bring your own key.
[03:15] Priya Narayanan: Good. For logging and auditing, do you surface token-level traces? We need to correlate latency spikes to customer requests.
[03:25] Maya Chen: Console has token-level breakdowns and per-route latency. We can stream audit logs to your SIEM. For the pilot we can enable verbose tracing for a window.
[03:40] Emily Stone: Ok nice. Diego, our busiest windows are 09:00-10:30 and 16:30-17:15 PST, with microbursts inside those windows. I'll share heatmaps after this.
[03:55] Diego Ramos: Yep, heatmap will show those 90-minute blocks.
[04:05] Raj Patel: Helpful — can you also include p50/p95/p99 distributions and payload size? That drives kernel selection and batching behavior.
[04:15] Emily Stone: Will do.

[04:30] Technical deep dive snippet:
[04:30] Raj Patel: On prewarm sizing we'd recommend sizing to the sustained baseline QPS and then a small buffer for average burst length. If your typical burst lasts 30-90s, a hot-pool with a fast spin-up policy covers that without paying for full reservations for the whole time.
[04:52] Priya Narayanan: How long to spin up a new node from cold?
[04:58] Raj Patel: Cold start to first token is model and image-dependent, typically 30-90s for large models. With our prewarm it can be under 10s since the runtime is already initialized and KV cache warming starts faster.
[05:18] Emily Stone: So for our 350 qps microburst, you'd want X reserved plus Y prewarm?
[05:24] Raj Patel: Rough guideline: reserve for steady 120 qps, keep hotpool sized for 100-150 qps and have autoscaling to pull from spot-like capacity for the rest. We'll run numbers after we see your heatmap.

[05:50] Security and compliance:
[05:50] Maya Chen: On encryption, we support customer-managed KMS keys and can keep model artifacts in customer-controlled buckets for Private deployments. SOC2 report is in the pack I'll send.
[06:05] Emily Stone: Do you support SAML SSO and SSO ephemeral tokens for console ops?
[06:10] Maya Chen: Yes SAML and SCIM for provisioning, RBAC controls at team/model level. We can also restrict console access to IP allowlist.
[06:22] Priya Narayanan: What about data residency — our legal team asks that certain workloads stay in EU regions.
[06:28] Raj Patel: You can pin routes and models to specific regions; Dedicated and Private deployments let you control physical region. For Hosted, you can choose region endpoints with data residency guarantees.

[06:45] Cost discussion and quantization:
[06:45] Diego Ramos: We want to explore quantized variants for lower cost. Does Redwood do 8-bit/4-bit quantization and what's the quality delta?
[06:55] Raj Patel: We support multiple quantization profiles; 8-bit often gives minimal quality loss for embedding and many completion use-cases. 4-bit is aggressive — depends on your prompt sensitivity. We can run AB tests and link regression alerts to your evals.
[07:15] Emily Stone: Perfect, we have eval sets. Would be great if we can gate rollouts on eval pass/fail.
[07:22] Maya Chen: That's exactly our Optimize feature — you can run a canary and automatically rollback if quality dips.

[07:40] Pilot shape and contract:
[07:40] Maya Chen: For a pilot, standard approach: 1-3 month reserved baseline sized to your steady QPS, include a small hot-pool for prewarm, and allow burst into opportunistic capacity. We provide a performance SLO during pilot and run a joint synthetic test.
[07:58] Diego Ramos: Pricing — ballpark per GPU-hour and any uplift for isolation?
[08:03] Maya Chen: I'll send ballpark numbers. Physical isolated clusters carry a modest uplift to cover dedicated provisioning. We'll include that in the pilot draft.

[08:20] Questions from Orchard:
[08:20] Priya Narayanan: How do you handle tenant fencing in multi-tenant racks? Can noisy neighbor VM-level processes be killed?
[08:28] Raj Patel: We do strict cgroup and runtime fencing; compute isolation enforced by hypervisor/container boundaries. For highest guarantee, dedicated racks/nodes remove co-tenancy entirely.
[08:40] Emily Stone: Any telemetry overhead from verbose logging? We can't add too much latency.
[08:46] Raj Patel: Tracing is configurable. You can enable verbose mode only for a small sample or a short window.

[09:05] Live troubleshooting scenario:
[09:05] Emily Stone: If we see a p99 spike during the 09:00 window, what's the playbook — auto-scale or fallback?
[09:12] Raj Patel: Auto-scale first to hotpool, then fallback to a smaller quantized model for new requests while existing sessions finish. For critical flows we can apply throttling policies and shaped queues.
[09:28] Diego Ramos: And grace for in-flight KV cache? Won't fallback models miss the warmed cache leading to more latency?
[09:36] Raj Patel: Correct, cache loss can cost time. Our routing tries to stick to warmed pools for stateful session traffic, and we use prefix-KV caching to reduce cold penalty. For sessions we can pin a session to an instance to preserve cache during a short burst.

[09:58] Operational readiness:
[09:58] Maya Chen: We'll also want service-level runbooks: who to page, what metrics to watch, and a joint runbook for failover. For pilot, Raj can help set the SLO thresholds.
[10:12] Priya Narayanan: Who owns the runbook updates? Orchard or Redwood?
[10:16] Maya Chen: It's collaborative; we'll draft then iterate. Usually Redwood owns the platform runbook and Orchard owns app-level triggers.

[10:35] Closing and next steps recap:
[10:35] Maya Chen: Recap — Orchard will share heatmaps and p99 traces, Redwood will provide sizing and pilot pricing. We'll schedule a 60 minute VPC/KMS deep dive with Priya next week.
[10:48] Emily Stone: Sounds good. Also please include the SOC2 summary and the KMS integration guide in the email.
[10:55] Maya Chen: Will do. Raj any final technical notes?
[10:59] Raj Patel: I'll prepare a sizing spreadsheet and a sample synthetic test plan for the pilot traffic profile.
[11:05] Diego Ramos: OK thanks all, looking forward to the pilot.
[11:08] Maya Chen: Thanks, talk soon.
